article.title: Thread runout, relief and geometric runout: different drawing requirements
article.metaTitle: Thread Runout vs Relief vs Geometric Runout | ZUFEK
article.description: Distinguish incomplete thread regions, relief grooves and datum-based geometric runout. Define seating clearance, usable engagement and separate acceptance checks.
article.intro: Thread runout can name the incomplete-thread region at the end of a threaded length. Circular or total runout is a separate geometric-tolerance requirement. A drawing should distinguish these meanings, then define any relief groove, usable full thread and seating clearance needed by the assembly.
checklist: Full-thread length and its reference face
Mating chamfer, counterbore or clearance envelope
Separate datum and tolerance for any geometric runout
article.example: Illustrative assembly: a collar must seat against a screw shoulder. Review the collar bore, its entry chamfer and the permitted incomplete-thread region together. A relief may provide clearance, but its section and radius also require design review. A separate geometric-runout callout is considered only if the functional relationship between surfaces requires it. No particular clearance, torque or test result is assumed.
sections: An incomplete thread region is where the thread profile is not fully formed near its end. A relief or undercut is a deliberately machined or formed reduced section. Geometric runout controls variation of a specified surface relative to a datum axis. These requirements can coexist on one component, but an axial incomplete-thread length is not a circular-runout tolerance.
Define usable thread before evaluating the transition

Specify the thread system, pitch, tolerance class where applicable and the required usable full-thread length. Identify the reference face and the allowed location of the incomplete region. A visible threaded length can include incomplete profile at an end; it should not be assumed to provide the same usable engagement throughout. Show the mating component when seating depends on this transition.
Check the mating clearance rather than adding a groove by habit

A shoulder, collar, receiving thread or counterbore can interfere with incomplete thread before the intended face seats. Compare the permitted transition envelope with the mating bore, chamfer and axial stack. Where a relief is needed, define its diameter, axial width and transition radius. Review the remaining section with the responsible designer; a clearance groove can also change the local stress condition.
Specify geometric runout only as a separate functional requirement

If the assembly requires control of a surface as the part rotates about a reference axis, identify the controlled surface, datum reference and the selected geometric tolerance. State circular or total runout as appropriate to the drawing system and function. Do not use that datum-based check as a substitute for the permitted axial length of incomplete thread, or impose it merely because the word runout appears in a thread note.
Match each requirement to its own check

A suitable profile or dimensional method can evaluate an accessible incomplete-thread region and relief geometry against the drawing. Thread gauges address their specified thread acceptance and do not automatically verify seating clearance. Geometric runout needs a setup referenced to the required datum axis. A controlled mating-part trial can support seating evaluation, with its revision and limits recorded separately.
Make the quotation and release decision explicit

Ask the supplier to identify any tool-exit allowance, proposed relief or unresolved transition detail before sample approval. Record acceptance in the final supplied condition when treatment can affect the interface. Release the drawing only after usable thread, seating clearance and any independent geometric requirement are unambiguous. The comparison and example describe a review method, not universal dimensions or a certified design.
